findings.claim: The First Witch describes how she has shipwrecked a sailor's husband because his wife refused to share her chestnuts.
findings.truth: The sailor IS the husband, and the witch says she cannot wreck him: 'Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.' She plans to deny him sleep and waste him away.
findings.evidence: Macbeth 1.3: 'A sailor's wife had chestnuts in her lap... Her husband's to Aleppo gone, master o' th' Tiger... Though his bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost.'

findings.claim: King James I, who claimed descent from the historical Banquo.
findings.truth: Banquo is not a historical figure. James believed himself descended from Banquo; the Stuarts in fact descend from a Breton family that reached Scotland later.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macbeth - 'In the 19th century it was established that Banquo is an unhistorical character'

findings.claim: The metaphor of pouring poison into someone’s ear echoes the biblical story of the serpent tempting Eve.
findings.truth: Lady Macbeth says she will pour her 'spirits', not poison, in Macbeth's ear, and poison-in-the-ear is a Hamlet image, not a Genesis one. The serpent link is made correctly later in the same lesson, so the claim is loose rather than damaging. Left for a human call; an edit here would ripple through narration block n3 for little gain.
findings.evidence: Macbeth 1.5 line 703: 'That I may pour my spirits in thine ear'

findings.claim: He compares himself to a wolf (“withered murder, / Alarumed by his sentinel, the wolf”) and to Tarquin...
findings.truth: Macbeth does not compare himself to the wolf. The wolf is Murder's sentinel, whose howl wakes Murder; it is Murder that moves 'With Tarquin's ravishing strides'.
findings.evidence: Macbeth 2.1: 'wither'd murder, / Alarum'd by his sentinel, the wolf, / Whose howl's his watch... With Tarquin's ravishing strides, towards his design / Moves like a ghost.'

findings.claim: Macbeth’s final words are a rhyming couplet: [three lines quoted]
findings.truth: A couplet is two lines. The three quoted lines end in a couplet (knell / hell). Changed 'are a' to 'end in a'.

findings.claim: trochaic tetrameter: 'A metrical pattern of two stressed syllables in a row, used here to create a chanting, ritualistic effect.'
findings.truth: That describes a spondee. A trochee is a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one, and tetrameter means four feet to the line. The wrong definition sits in the glossary, the flashcard and the in-text definition, so all three are corrected.
findings.evidence: standard prosody; the lesson's own claim that the witches differ from iambic pentameter only works with the correct definition

findings.claim: King James I, who was in the audience at early performances and who claimed descent from Banquo.
findings.truth: No record places James at an early performance of Macbeth; the 1606 court performance is a tradition, not evidence. Banquo is also unhistorical. Softened to what James believed.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macbeth - no documented court performance; Banquo unhistorical

findings.claim: Shakespeare was influenced by Aristotle’s writings on Greek tragedy.
findings.truth: There is no evidence Shakespeare read the Poetics, and he breaks the Aristotelian unities freely. Hamartia, peripeteia and anagnorisis are terms later critics apply to the play. Reworded to say exactly that; the three terms are kept.
findings.evidence: Internet Shakespeare Editions, 'Aristotle on tragedy': the Poetics shaped Renaissance critics such as Sidney and Jonson, and Shakespeare probably did not know Greek tragedy directly

findings.claim: Match option: ‘I have no spur to prick the sides of my intent, only vaulting ambition’
findings.truth: The line runs 'I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition'. The elision is silent and the sense is unchanged, so it is not worth an edit, but it is a compressed quotation presented as verbatim.

summary: Every quotation, speaker and act/scene reference was checked against the Gutenberg text and every exam claim against the spec; the exam facts (extract printed, whole play, closed book, 30 marks plus 4 for spelling and grammar) are right throughout. The real damage is elsewhere: two places name the exam board (one pastes a past-paper question), five auto-generated flashcards are mangled or duplicate an answer inside their own deck, three quotations are misattributed or invented, 'incarnadine' is misspelt, and the definition of trochaic tetrameter describes a spondee.
